slides.say: P D and P E are tangent to the circle at D and E. A lies on the major arc D E. Given: angle D P E is sixty-eight degrees. What is angle D A E?
at: P D and P E are tangent

slides.say: We know one angle, outside the circle, and we want an angle at A, on the circle. [short pause] We'll go from P to the center, and from the center to A. There's also a second way, with symmetry.

[short pause] Let's start with the math way. Here's the figure again, bigger. We have tangents to a circle, so the first thing we do is draw the radii to the points of tangency, O D and O E. The radius is perpendicular to the tangent, so we get ninety degrees, twice. Make that a habit. Tangents, then radii, then right angles.
at: draw the radii to the points

slides.say: Now I have a quadrilateral, O D P E, with the center as one of its corners. The angles of a quadrilateral add up to three hundred sixty.
at: add up to three hundred sixty

slides.say: The two right angles already give a hundred eighty. So the other two angles need another hundred eighty. Sixty-eight plus the angle at O is a hundred eighty. So the central angle is a hundred eighty minus sixty-eight, which is a hundred twelve.
at: The two right angles already give
Sixty-eight plus the angle at O

slides.say: Careful, a hundred twelve is in the choices, but it's the central angle, not the angle we want. We're not done yet.
Now it's very easy. Stand at A and look between the two lines, A D and A E. You see the short arc D E, the same arc the central angle sees.

So the angle at A is an inscribed angle on the same arc as the hundred twelve. An inscribed angle is half of the central angle. Half of a hundred twelve is fifty-six. Choice number four is our answer.
at: Choice number four is our answer

slides.say: This is worth remembering. With two tangents from one point P, the shape O D P E always has two right angles. So the angle at P and the central angle D O E always add up to a hundred eighty. Here, sixty-eight plus a hundred twelve. With an angle of forty at P, the central angle would be a hundred forty.
at: always add up to a hundred eighty

slides.say: [pause] Now the second way, by understanding, with symmetry. We start again from the radii and the right angles. O D P E is a kite, because the radii are equal and the two tangents from P are equal. So let's draw its line of symmetry, O P.
at: We start again from the radii
let's draw its line of symmetry

slides.say: The line of symmetry cuts the angle at P into two equal halves. Half of sixty-eight is thirty-four. So each half is thirty-four.
Careful, thirty-four is in the choices too. It's half of the angle at P, and that's not angle D A E.
at: and that's not angle D A E

slides.say: Now look at the right triangle O D P. Its angles add up to a hundred eighty. A hundred eighty minus ninety is ninety. Ninety minus thirty-four is fifty-six. So angle D O P is fifty-six.
at: Now look at the right triangle
So angle D O P is fifty-six

slides.say: By the same symmetry, O P also cuts the central angle D O E in half. So fifty-six is half of the central angle. And the inscribed angle at A is also half of the central angle. So angle D A E is fifty-six again, choice number four. Either way, it all started with the radii to the points of tangency. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next question.
at: So fifty-six is half of the central angle
So angle D A E is fifty-six
